paragraphs.context: While I was trying to decide what to do for book number nine
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer says children asked her to send Jack and Annie under the sea.
paragraphs.simple: When the writer was thinking about book nine, many children asked her to send Jack and Annie under the ocean.

paragraphs.context: After a number of kids suggested a submarine
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children gave her the idea of a mini-sub.
paragraphs.simple: She asked how Jack and Annie could breathe and talk under water. Many children said: use a submarine. So she read about small submarines, and then she knew what to do.

background.note: A mini-sub is a very small submarine. It carries only one to three people. Scientists use mini-subs to study the deep sea.

paragraphs.context: So, thanks to all the kids who’ve helped me
paragraphs.mainIdea: The writer thanks children for their ideas.
paragraphs.simple: She thanks all the children who help her with ideas. She feels that she, the readers, Jack and Annie are all on these adventures together.
paragraphs.tone: The writer talks to the reader like a friend. She wants you to feel that you are part of the story.

paragraphs.context: Jack had been awake for a long time.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack had a dream about Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.simple: Jack woke up very early. He kept thinking about his dream. In the dream, Morgan le Fay spoke to him.

background.note: Morgan le Fay comes from old British stories about King Arthur. In these books she is a magic librarian. Her magic tree house takes Jack and Annie to other places and times.

paragraphs.context: The tree house is back, Morgan had said. I’m waiting.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan said in the dream that the tree house had come back.
paragraphs.simple: In the dream Morgan said: "The tree house is back. I am waiting for you."
paragraphs.tone: The words are in a different style in the book because they are Morgan's words from the dream, not real talk.

paragraphs.context: He raced up the stairs. Having the same dream must mean something
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks the same dream must be important.
paragraphs.simple: Jack ran up the stairs very fast. He thought: we both had the same dream, so it must mean something.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie ran up their quiet street to the Frog Creek woods.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The children run to the woods.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie ran up their quiet street to the woods near their home.

background.note: Frog Creek is the made-up small town where Jack and Annie live, in Pennsylvania, USA. A creek is a small river.

paragraphs.context: They headed between the trees. Soon they came to the tallest oak
paragraphs.mainIdea: They find the tree house in the tallest tree.
paragraphs.simple: They walked into the woods. Soon they came to the tallest oak tree. High in the top of the tree there was a small wooden house.

paragraphs.context: Someone looked out the window of the tree house
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan le Fay is in the tree house.
paragraphs.simple: A lovely old woman with long white hair looked out of the tree house window. It was Morgan le Fay.

paragraphs.context: In the dawn light, they stared at Morgan le Fay.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They look at Morgan in the early morning light.
paragraphs.simple: In the early morning light, the children looked at Morgan. She looked beautiful in a long, soft, red coat.

paragraphs.context: “Merlin the Magician has been up to his tricks again,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan is busy with Merlin, so she needs help.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said: "Merlin has been playing his tricks again. So I had no time to find books for the library in Camelot."

background.note: Merlin is a famous magic man from the old stories about King Arthur. In these books he likes to play tricks.
Camelot is the castle and town of King Arthur in old British stories. Morgan collects books for its library.

paragraphs.context: “Yes, but in order to gather books through time you must be Master Librarians,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: To collect books, the children must become Master Librarians.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said: "Yes, you can help. But to collect books from different times, you must first be Master Librarians."

background.note: A made-up title in this series. It means very good librarians who know how to find answers in books. Jack and Annie must pass a test to get it.

paragraphs.context: “You must show that you know how to do research,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The test: show you can do research and answer hard questions.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said: "You must show that you can study to find facts, and that you can find answers to hard questions."

paragraphs.context: “By solving four riddles,” said Morgan.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan gives them the first of four riddles.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan said they must answer four riddles. She took a rolled paper out of her long coat.

paragraphs.context: “The first riddle is written on this ancient scroll,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: The first riddle is on a very old paper. A book will help.
paragraphs.simple: She said: "The first riddle is on this very old rolled paper. This book will help you find the answer."

background.note: A scroll is a long paper that is rolled up. Before people had books like ours, they often wrote on scrolls.

paragraphs.context: “You will know,” Morgan said mysteriously.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Morgan promises they will know the right answer.
paragraphs.simple: Morgan did not explain. She said in a secret way: "You will know. I promise."

paragraphs.context: A breeze blew through the window. Sea gulls cried.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They are now by the sea.
paragraphs.simple: A soft wind came in through the window. Sea birds called. Small waves came softly onto the land again and again.

background.note: Gulls are large grey and white birds that live by the sea. Their calls are loud, so the book says they "cried".

paragraphs.context: Rough and gray as rock,
paragraphs.mainIdea: This is the riddle.
paragraphs.simple: The riddle says: I am rough and grey like a rock. I am very plain. But deep inside me there is something very beautiful. What am I?
paragraphs.tone: A riddle talks like a person ("I") so that you must guess what it is. Each line is a clue.

paragraphs.context: This is a coral reef. Corals are tiny sea animals.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The ocean book explains what a coral reef is.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: This is a coral reef. Corals are very small sea animals. When they die, their hard bodies stay. Over many years, the reef grows from many piles of these bodies.

background.note: A coral reef is a long place under warm, clear sea water, made of coral. It looks like rock, but it was made by millions of tiny animals. It is home to many fish. The biggest one in the world is near Australia.

paragraphs.context: She was standing at the edge of the water.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie finds a strange machine by the water.
paragraphs.simple: Annie stood where the water started. Next to her was a strange machine.

paragraphs.context: The machine was half on the reef and half in the clear blue water.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The machine looks like a big white bubble.
paragraphs.simple: Half of the machine was on the reef, and half was in the clear blue water. It looked like a big white ball of air with a big window.

paragraphs.context: Scientists who study the ocean are called oceanographers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains what a mini-sub is.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: Scientists who study the sea are called oceanographers. Sometimes they go in small boats that can go under water, called mini-subs, to study the bottom of the sea.

background.note: Ocean + -grapher (a person who writes about or studies something). These scientists study sea water, sea animals and the sea floor.
From "submerge", to go under water. A submersible is a small machine that can go under water, like a mini-sub.

paragraphs.context: No!” said Jack. Actually, he did want to see what the sub looked like inside.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack wants to look too, but he says no.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said no. But really he did want to see inside. He shook his head and said: "We can't. It is not ours."
paragraphs.tone: Jack says no, but he wants to say yes. This is often how Jack is: careful, but curious.

paragraphs.context: “Just a teeny peek,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie wants to look inside the mini-sub.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said: "Just a very small, quick look. It might help us answer the riddle."
paragraphs.tone: "Teeny" is a word children use for "very, very small". Annie is trying to make it sound like no big thing.

paragraphs.context: He and Annie slipped off their shoes and socks
paragraphs.mainIdea: They take off their shoes.
paragraphs.simple: They quickly took off their shoes and socks and threw them toward the tree house, so they would stay dry.

paragraphs.context: The mini-sub was tiny. Two seats faced the big window.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The inside of the mini-sub.
paragraphs.simple: The mini-sub was very small. There were two seats in front of the big window. In front of the seats was a computer, as part of a board with buttons.

paragraphs.context: Mini-subs have strong hulls to keep air in
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains how a mini-sub keeps people safe.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: Mini-subs have a strong body. It keeps air inside and keeps the people inside safe from the strong push of the deep water. Computers help to drive the mini-sub.

background.note: Deep in the sea, all the water above you pushes down very hard. A person could not live there without a strong sub.

paragraphs.context: An air blower came on. The mini-sub jerked backward.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mini-sub starts to move.
paragraphs.simple: A machine that blows air started. The mini-sub moved back suddenly.

paragraphs.context: He and Annie scrambled for the hatch.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They try to get out, but it is too late.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie hurried to the small door. Jack took hold of the handle.

paragraphs.context: Then it dove silently down into the deep.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The mini-sub goes down into the sea.
paragraphs.simple: Then, with no sound, the mini-sub went down into the deep sea.

paragraphs.context: “We have to get back to the reef,” said Jack. His eyes were still glued
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is worried about the owners of the mini-sub.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said they had to go back to the reef. He could not stop looking at the computer screen. He asked: "What if the owners come and find the sub is not there?"

paragraphs.context: The mini-sub was moving past red, yellow, and blue coral
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see a wonderful world under the sea.
paragraphs.simple: The mini-sub moved past colourful coral. The coral looked like small mountains, valleys and caves. There were fish of every colour and size.

paragraphs.context: Jack nodded slowly. She might be right, he thought.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack agrees to stay a little.
paragraphs.simple: Jack nodded. He thought Annie might be right. And when would they ever have the chance to visit a place like this again?

paragraphs.context: There were fish everywhere: floating over the swaying sea grass
paragraphs.mainIdea: Fish are everywhere.
paragraphs.simple: There were fish everywhere. Some were moving slowly above the sea grass. Some were eating on the sand at the bottom. Some were looking out of small coral caves.

paragraphs.context: Some kinds of coral looked like blue fingers or lacy fans.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The coral has many shapes.
paragraphs.simple: Some coral looked like blue fingers or pretty fans. Other coral looked like the horns of a deer, or leaves of a salad plant, or mushrooms, or trees.

paragraphs.context: Coral reefs are only found in warm, tropical waters.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells where coral reefs are.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: Coral reefs are only in warm seas in hot parts of the world. Almost 5,000 kinds of fish live around coral reefs in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.

background.note: The tropical parts of the world are the hot places near the middle of the Earth, like the south of China's Hainan Island and the seas around it.
The Pacific Ocean is the biggest sea in the world, east of China. The Indian Ocean is south of India.

paragraphs.context: Jack saw a creature that looked like a giant pancake with a long tail.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see a stingray.
paragraphs.simple: Jack saw an animal that looked like a very big, flat, round cake with a long tail. It was a stingray.

paragraphs.context: The giant clam of the coral reef is three feet wide
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells about the giant clam.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: The giant clam is about 90 centimetres wide and can weigh about 90 kilos.

background.note: The USA uses feet and pounds. One foot is about 30 centimetres. One pound is about 0.45 kilos. So 200 pounds is about 90 kilos, as heavy as a big man.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up. Two dolphins were peering in the window.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Two dolphins look in at them.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked up. Two dolphins were looking in the window. They hit the glass softly with their noses.

background.note: Dolphins live in the sea but they are not fish. They breathe air and feed milk to their babies. They are very clever and often seem to smile.

paragraphs.context: Jack laughed. “It’s like we’re in a fish tank
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack makes a joke about who is looking at whom.
paragraphs.simple: Jack laughed. He said it was like they were the fish in a glass box, and the dolphins were the people looking at them.
paragraphs.tone: This is a funny idea. Usually people look at fish, but here the dolphins look at the people.

paragraphs.context: “Here’s a kiss for you, Sukie,” Annie said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie gives the dolphin a kiss through the glass.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said: "Here is a kiss for you, Sukie." She put her lips on the glass, as if she was kissing the dolphin's nose.
paragraphs.tone: Annie loves animals and gives them names at once. Jack thinks she is silly ("Oh, brother").

paragraphs.context: “You forgot the ‘rough as a rock’ part,” said Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack says dolphins cannot be the answer.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said: "You forgot the part about rough like a rock. Dolphin skin looks smooth and wet, not rough."

paragraphs.context: It’s a diary of an ocean trip
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack explains what a ship's log is.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said a ship's log is like a diary of a trip on the sea.

background.note: On a ship, the captain writes down each day where the ship went and what happened. This is called the ship's log.

paragraphs.context: “ ‘Defective’ means broken, right?” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They learn the sub is broken.
paragraphs.simple: Annie asked if "defective" means broken. Jack said yes.

paragraphs.context: “Yep,” said Jack. “And it was waiting to be taken away by a helicopter.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The broken sub was going to be thrown away.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said: "Yes. And it was waiting for a helicopter to take it away, to a place for old broken things."

paragraphs.context: Two eyes were staring out from behind a giant sea plant.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They see two big eyes.
paragraphs.simple: Two eyes were looking out from behind a very big sea plant. They looked like people's eyes, but they were as big as golf balls.

background.note: A golf ball is a small hard white ball, about 4 centimetres across. That is very big for an eye.

paragraphs.context: Then another—and another—and another
paragraphs.mainIdea: Arm after arm comes out.
paragraphs.simple: Then more and more arms came out, one after another, eight in all.
paragraphs.tone: The writer repeats "and another" again and again. This makes you feel the fear grow as each new arm comes out.

paragraphs.context: Jack and Annie stared in horror at a giant octopus.
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is a giant octopus.
paragraphs.simple: Jack and Annie looked with great fear at a very big octopus.

background.note: An octopus is a sea animal with a soft body and eight arms. The giant Pacific octopus can be more than 4 metres across.

paragraphs.context: Slowly, the octopus crept through the water.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The octopus comes to the mini-sub.
paragraphs.simple: Slowly and quietly, the octopus moved through the water. Its eight arms reached out for the mini-sub.

paragraphs.context: The octopus hugged the mini-sub. Each of its eight arms had two rows of suckers.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The octopus holds the mini-sub.
paragraphs.simple: The octopus put its arms around the mini-sub. Each arm had two lines of round cups. The cups stuck to the window.

paragraphs.context: The octopus tends to be a gentle, shy creature.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says the octopus is usually shy.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: An octopus is usually a kind and shy animal. But sometimes it wants to know about something so much that it comes out of its hiding place.

paragraphs.context: But the octopus has huge strength.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book says the octopus is very strong.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: But the octopus is very strong. Each of its arms has many round cups that work like rubber cups that stick to glass. It is almost impossible to get something away from its arms.
paragraphs.tone: Jack reads this in fear. "Oh, great" means "Oh, this is very bad."

paragraphs.context: A thin crack ran along the ceiling.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sub is breaking.
paragraphs.simple: A thin broken line went across the top of the sub. Smaller lines went out from it. Water came in, drop by drop.

paragraphs.context: “Get out of here!” Jack yelled at it.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack shouts at the octopus.
paragraphs.simple: Jack shouted: "Go away! Now! Go away! Go away! Go!"
paragraphs.tone: Annie is polite with the octopus, but Jack shouts many rude ways to say "go away". It is funny because they are so different.

paragraphs.context: The octopus shot a cloud of black liquid into the water
paragraphs.mainIdea: The octopus leaves in a cloud of ink.
paragraphs.simple: The octopus pushed out a cloud of black liquid. It went into the dark cloud and was gone. Its long arms moved behind it in the water.

paragraphs.context: The octopus squirts black ink to escape its enemies.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack learns why the octopus left.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: The octopus shoots out black ink to get away from animals that want to eat it. One of these is the shark.

background.note: An octopus has a bag of dark ink in its body. When it is afraid, it shoots the ink out. The other animal cannot see, and the octopus swims away.

paragraphs.context: The fish was way bigger than the dolphins.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A big fish with a strange head comes.
paragraphs.simple: The fish was much bigger than the dolphins. And it had a very strange head.

paragraphs.context: “A hammerhead shark,” he breathed.
paragraphs.mainIdea: It is a hammerhead shark.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said very quietly: "A hammerhead shark. Now we are really in trouble."

background.note: A kind of shark with a very wide, flat head, like a hammer. Its eyes are at the two ends of its head. Big ones can be dangerous.

paragraphs.context: Jack looked up. The water wasn’t dripping now—it was spurting.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Water comes in fast now.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked up. The water was not coming in drop by drop now. It was coming in fast.

paragraphs.context: Suddenly, the mini-sub burst out of the water.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The sub comes up to the top of the sea.
paragraphs.simple: Suddenly the mini-sub came up out of the water. It moved up and down on the waves like a light piece of wood. The sea was shining all around it.

paragraphs.context: “Right,” said Annie. “It’s a good thing we had swimming lessons this summer.”
paragraphs.mainIdea: They must swim.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said it was good that they had learned to swim in the summer.

paragraphs.context: If you ever see a shark in the water, don’t splash.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells what to do if you see a shark.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: If you see a shark in the water, don't hit the water and make it fly up. Swim away slowly and quietly.

background.note: Splashing makes noise and moves the water. A shark may think you are a hurt fish and come to you.

paragraphs.context: “We better do the breast stroke,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie picks a quiet way to swim.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said they should swim the breast stroke so they would not make the water fly up.

background.note: A way of swimming. Your arms and legs move out to the sides, like a frog. It is slow and quiet.

paragraphs.context: Jack took a deep breath. He tried to be calm, too.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack tries very hard to be calm.
paragraphs.simple: Jack breathed in deeply and tried to stay calm. He took off his glasses calmly. He put them and the book into his bag calmly. He put the bag on his back calmly.
paragraphs.tone: The word "calmly" comes again and again. This is funny: Jack is really very afraid, so he must tell himself again and again to be calm.

paragraphs.context: “Help,” Jack said calmly. He held his nose.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack goes into the sea.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said "Help" in a calm voice. He held his nose and went down into the sea.
paragraphs.tone: This is a joke. People shout "Help!" when they are afraid, but Jack says it calmly.

paragraphs.context: Then Jack saw something out of the corner of his eye.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack sees something at the side.
paragraphs.simple: Then Jack saw something at the side of his eyes, not right in front of him.
hardWords: out of the corner of his eye

paragraphs.context: A dark fin was zigzagging through the water.
paragraphs.mainIdea: A shark's fin comes toward them.
paragraphs.simple: A dark fin was moving left and right through the water. It was coming toward them.

background.note: A shark has a big fin on its back. When a shark swims near the top of the sea, you can see the fin above the water.

paragraphs.context: I better not tell Annie, he thought.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not tell Annie about the shark.
paragraphs.simple: Jack thought: I should not tell Annie. She will be calmer if she does not know.

paragraphs.context: Jack was so scared that he wasn’t tired at all.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack swims for his life.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was so afraid that he did not feel tired. He was swimming as fast as he could to stay alive, and to keep Annie alive too.

paragraphs.context: But the more Jack floated, the more tired he felt.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack is too tired and starts to go down.
paragraphs.simple: The longer Jack lay on the water, the more tired he felt. Soon he was too tired even to lie on the water. He started to go down.

paragraphs.context: His heart stopped. Something pushed at him in the water.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Something touches Jack.
paragraphs.simple: Jack was very afraid. Something pushed him in the water.

paragraphs.context: Jack shut his eyes and waited for the worst.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack waits for something very bad.
paragraphs.simple: Jack closed his eyes and waited for the shark to attack. He waited a long time. At last he opened his eyes.

paragraphs.context: She was clinging to the fin of another dolphin!
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie is holding a dolphin's fin.
paragraphs.simple: Annie was holding on tightly to the fin of another dolphin. Her dolphin was swimming with her.

paragraphs.context: Then the two dolphins swam smoothly through the water
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dolphins take them to the reef.
paragraphs.simple: Then the two dolphins swam easily through the water. They pulled Jack and Annie toward the reef.

paragraphs.context: But Sam nuzzled Jack’s head. Then he put his flippers
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dolphin hugs Jack.
paragraphs.simple: But Sam pushed his nose softly against Jack's head. Then he put his flat arms around Jack's neck.

paragraphs.context: Jack couldn’t resist. He threw his arms around the dolphin
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack kisses the dolphin.
paragraphs.simple: Jack could not stop himself. He hugged the dolphin and gave him a quick kiss.
paragraphs.tone: Jack said Annie was "nuts" for kissing a dolphin. Now he does it too. This is sweet and funny.

paragraphs.context: The two dolphins chattered to each other for a moment.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dolphins leave.
paragraphs.simple: The two dolphins "talked" to each other for a short time. They nodded at Jack and Annie and swam away beautifully.

paragraphs.context: “I saw the shark when we were swimming,” Annie said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie also saw the shark but kept it a secret.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said she saw the shark too, but she did not tell Jack because she wanted him to stay calm.

paragraphs.context: Jack stared at her. “I saw it, too.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Both of them kept the same secret.
paragraphs.simple: Jack looked at her. He said he saw it too, and he swam faster so that she would swim faster.
paragraphs.tone: This is funny and kind: each one wanted to keep the other calm, so each swam faster for the other.

paragraphs.context: “I guess we swam double-fast then,” Jack said.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They swam twice as fast.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said: "So we swam two times as fast." He shook his head because it was so surprising.

paragraphs.context: “We’ve failed,” he said. “My research is all wet.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack thinks they have failed.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said: "We did not do it. My notes are all wet. We will never be Master Librarians now."
paragraphs.tone: "All wet" is a little joke: his notes really are wet, and in American talk "all wet" also means "all wrong".

paragraphs.context: She picked up a large gray shell.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie finds a rough grey shell.
paragraphs.simple: Annie picked up a large grey shell. She said: "It is very rough. Rough and grey like a rock—"

paragraphs.context: “And plain as plain can be!” whispered Jack.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They find the answer to the riddle.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said quietly: "And very plain!" The shell is just like the riddle. They found the answer.

paragraphs.context: The shell looked like a clamshell—only bigger and with more ridges.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The shell is like a clam shell.
paragraphs.simple: The shell looked like a clam shell, but it was bigger and had more raised lines on it.

paragraphs.context: Divers search for oysters in deep water.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book tells about oysters and pearls.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: Divers look for oysters in deep water. But sometimes waves carry oysters onto reefs or beaches. Inside some oysters there is a pearl. A pearl is beautiful without any help from people, so it is very special.

background.note: An oyster is a sea animal with a soft body inside a rough grey shell. It is often eaten as food.
A pearl is a small, round, shiny white ball that grows inside an oyster. People make necklaces and rings with pearls. In China, Guangxi and Hainan are famous for pearls.

paragraphs.context: Sometimes a grain of sand will get between the oyster’s shell and its skin.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The book explains how a pearl grows.
paragraphs.simple: The book says: Sometimes a very small piece of sand gets inside the shell. This hurts the oyster a little. So the oyster covers the sand with a shiny, white material. After a few years, this becomes a pearl.

paragraphs.context: “Now that would really irritate the oyster,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie makes a joke and they leave the oyster.
paragraphs.simple: Jack wants to break the shell on a rock. Annie says that would really hurt the oyster. So they decide to leave it alone.
paragraphs.tone: Annie uses the word "irritate" from the book as a joke. A grain of sand irritates an oyster, but a rock would be much worse.

paragraphs.context: In its place was one shimmering silver word:
paragraphs.mainIdea: A word shows on the scroll.
paragraphs.simple: Where the riddle was, there was now one shining silver word: OYSTER.

paragraphs.context: “And here’s the Pennsylvania book,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: They use the Pennsylvania book to go home.
paragraphs.simple: Annie found the book about Pennsylvania. She said: "Let's go home."

background.note: Pennsylvania is a state in the east of the USA. Frog Creek is there. The tree house always has a book with a picture of Frog Creek, so they can wish to go home.

paragraphs.context: No time at all had passed since they’d left. Day was breaking.
paragraphs.mainIdea: At home, no time has passed.
paragraphs.simple: At home no time had passed at all. It was still early morning.

background.term: No time at all had passed
background.note: This is a rule of the magic tree house: when they travel, time at home stops. So their mom and dad do not know they were away.

paragraphs.context: “You know, we should have found the answer to the riddle right away,”
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack says the answer was there all the time.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said they should have found the answer at once, because the oyster was on the reef from the beginning.

paragraphs.context: “Fun?” said Jack. “You call being squeezed by an octopus
paragraphs.mainIdea: Jack does not think it was fun.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said: "Fun? An octopus held us tightly and a shark ran after us. Do you call that fun?"
paragraphs.tone: Jack is surprised and a little funny. Annie always sees the good side of things.

paragraphs.context: Jack smiled. “Right,” he said. The dolphins made up for everything.
paragraphs.mainIdea: The dolphins made the bad parts OK.
paragraphs.simple: Jack smiled and agreed. The dolphins were so good that the bad parts did not matter any more.

paragraphs.context: “I guess they were the true pearl in the oyster,” said Annie.
paragraphs.mainIdea: Annie says the dolphins were the best part.
paragraphs.simple: Annie said the dolphins were like the real pearl inside the oyster: the most beautiful thing in a hard day.
paragraphs.tone: This is a beautiful idea. The trip was rough, like the oyster shell, but inside it was something lovely: the dolphins.

paragraphs.context: “Not one bit,” called Jack. Then he and Annie slipped up the stairs
paragraphs.mainIdea: They go up to change their clothes.
paragraphs.simple: Jack said their shoes were not wet at all. Then they went up the stairs quietly to change their wet clothes.
paragraphs.tone: This is a joke. Their shoes are dry, but the rest of them is very wet. Jack tells the truth, but not all of it.

sentences.context: While I was trying to decide what to do for book number nine, kids kept asking me to send Jack and Annie under the ocean.
sentences.simple: When I was thinking about book nine, children asked me again and again to send Jack and Annie under the sea.

parts.text: While I was trying to decide what to do for book number nine,
parts.meaning: When I was thinking about what to write in book nine,
children asked me again and again

parts.text: to send Jack and Annie under the ocean.
parts.meaning: to send Jack and Annie under the sea.

sentences.grammar: "While ..." at the start tells you the time. The main part comes after the comma. "Kept asking" means "asked again and again".

sentences.context: After a number of kids suggested a submarine, I began researching the subject and learned about mini-subs, and that settled it.
sentences.simple: Many children said: use a submarine. So I studied submarines and learned about mini-subs. Then I knew what to do.
sentences.main: I began researching and learned about mini-subs.

parts.text: After a number of kids suggested a submarine,
parts.meaning: Many children gave the idea of a submarine.
Then I started to study it
and I learned about very small submarines,
and then I knew what to do.

sentences.grammar: "A number of" means "many". "That settled it" means "that made me decide". Read each "and" as "and then".

sentences.context: So, thanks to all the kids who’ve helped me—and keep helping me.
sentences.simple: So thank you to all the children who helped me before and still help me now.

parts.text: So, thanks to all the kids
parts.meaning: So, thank you to all the children
who have helped me
and who still help me now.

sentences.grammar: "Who've" is "who have". The long line (—) adds an extra idea at the end.

sentences.context: “Yes, but in order to gather books through time you must be Master Librarians,” said Morgan.
sentences.simple: Morgan said: "Yes, but to collect books from different times in history, you must be Master Librarians."

parts.meaning: "Yes, but

parts.text: in order to gather books through time
parts.meaning: to collect books from many different times,

parts.text: you must be Master Librarians,” said Morgan.
parts.meaning: you must first be Master Librarians," Morgan said.

sentences.grammar: "In order to ..." tells you the reason or purpose, like "so that you can". Find the main part after it: "you must be ...".

sentences.context: “You must show that you know how to do research,” said Morgan, “and show that you can find answers to hard questions.”
sentences.simple: Morgan said they must show two things: that they can study to find facts, and that they can find answers to hard questions.

parts.text: “You must show that you know how to do research,”
parts.meaning: "You must show that you can study to find facts,"

parts.job: Who is speaking, in the middle.
parts.meaning: Morgan said,

parts.text: “and show that you can find answers to hard questions.”
parts.meaning: "and show that you can answer hard questions."

sentences.grammar: "Said Morgan" sits in the middle of her words. Jump over it and read the two parts together: "show that ... and show that ...".

sentences.context: After they die, their skeletons remain.
sentences.simple: When corals die, their hard bodies stay.

parts.meaning: When the corals die,
their hard bodies stay there.

sentences.grammar: "Remain" means "stay". "They" and "their" are the corals.

sentences.context: Over time, the reef builds up from stacks of coral skeletons.
sentences.simple: After many years, the reef grows bigger as more and more coral bodies pile up.

parts.meaning: Slowly, over many years,
the reef grows bigger
from piles of hard coral bodies.

sentences.grammar: "Over time" means "slowly, after a long time". "Builds up" means "grows as more is added".

sentences.context: Sometimes they travel in small diving vessels called submersibles, or “mini-subs,” to study the ocean floor.
sentences.simple: Sometimes these scientists go in small boats that go under water, called mini-subs, to study the bottom of the sea.
sentences.main: They travel in small diving vessels.

parts.text: Sometimes they travel in small diving vessels
parts.meaning: Sometimes the scientists go in small boats that can go under water
which have the name submersibles, or mini-subs,
to study the bottom of the sea.

sentences.grammar: "Called ..." gives the name of a thing. "Or" here means "another name for it is". "To study ..." tells you why.

sentences.context: Mini-subs have strong hulls to keep air in and protect those aboard from water pressure.
sentences.simple: Mini-subs have a strong body. It keeps air inside and keeps the people in the sub safe from the strong push of the water.

parts.meaning: Mini-subs have a strong body
to keep the air inside

parts.text: and protect those aboard from water pressure.
parts.meaning: and to keep the people inside safe from the strong push of the water.

sentences.grammar: "To keep ... and protect ..." gives two reasons. "Those aboard" means "the people who are in the sub".

sentences.context: The mini-sub was moving past red, yellow, and blue coral—past little coral mountains, valleys, and caves—past fishes of every color and size.
sentences.simple: The mini-sub moved past colourful coral, past small coral mountains, valleys and caves, and past fish of every colour and size.
sentences.main: The mini-sub was moving past many things.

parts.text: The mini-sub was moving past red, yellow, and blue coral
parts.job: Main part and the first thing.
parts.meaning: The mini-sub went past coral of many colours,

parts.text: —past little coral mountains, valleys, and caves
parts.meaning: past coral shaped like small mountains, valleys and caves,

parts.text: —past fishes of every color and size.
parts.meaning: and past fish of every colour and size.

sentences.grammar: The word "past" comes three times. Each long line (—) gives one more thing they see. This makes you feel how much there is to see.

sentences.context: There were fish everywhere: floating over the swaying sea grass, eating on the white sandy bottom, peeping out of coral caves.
sentences.simple: There were fish everywhere. Some moved slowly over the sea grass. Some ate on the sand. Some looked out of coral caves.

parts.meaning: There were fish everywhere.

parts.text: floating over the swaying sea grass,
parts.meaning: Some moved slowly over the sea grass, which moved from side to side.

parts.text: eating on the white sandy bottom,
parts.meaning: Some ate on the white sand at the bottom.
Some looked out of small coral caves.

sentences.grammar: The ":" means "here is more about it". Each "-ing" part tells you what some of the fish were doing.

sentences.context: Others looked like deer antlers or lettuce leaves or mushrooms or trees.
sentences.simple: Other coral looked like deer horns, or salad leaves, or mushrooms, or trees.

parts.job: Main part. "Others" means other kinds of coral.
parts.meaning: Other coral looked like

parts.text: deer antlers or lettuce leaves or mushrooms or trees.
parts.meaning: deer horns, salad leaves, mushrooms or trees.

sentences.grammar: "Others" stands for "other kinds of coral", from the sentence before. The word "or" joins the list.

sentences.context: Nearly 5,000 different species of fish live around coral reefs in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
sentences.simple: Almost 5,000 kinds of fish live around the coral reefs in the Indian Ocean and the Pacific Ocean.
sentences.main: Nearly 5,000 species of fish live around coral reefs.

parts.meaning: Almost 5,000 kinds of fish
live near coral reefs

parts.text: in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
parts.meaning: in the Indian Ocean and the Pacific Ocean.

sentences.grammar: "Nearly" means "almost". "Species" means "kinds". "Indian and Pacific Oceans" means two seas, so "Oceans" has -s.

sentences.context: She pressed her lips to the glass as if she were kissing the dolphin’s nose.
sentences.simple: She put her lips on the glass, like she was kissing the dolphin's nose.
sentences.main: She pressed her lips to the glass.

parts.text: She pressed her lips to the glass
parts.meaning: She put her lips on the glass

parts.text: as if she were kissing the dolphin’s nose.
parts.meaning: like she was giving the dolphin's nose a kiss.

sentences.grammar: "As if" means "like". After "as if", English often uses "were" even for "she": it shows it is not really true.

sentences.context: Two eyes were staring out from behind a giant sea plant.
sentences.simple: Two eyes looked out from behind a very big sea plant.

parts.meaning: Two eyes were looking out

parts.text: from behind a giant sea plant.
parts.meaning: from the back of a very big sea plant.

sentences.grammar: "From behind" means it came from the other side of the plant.

sentences.context: They looked human—except they were as big as golf balls.
sentences.simple: They looked like people's eyes, but they were as big as golf balls.

parts.meaning: They looked like people's eyes

parts.text: —except they were as big as golf balls.
parts.job: The one thing that was different.
parts.meaning: but they were as big as golf balls.

sentences.grammar: "Except" means "but not in this one way". "As big as" compares two things.

sentences.context: Sometimes, though, curiosity gets the best of it and it comes out of hiding.
sentences.simple: But sometimes it wants to know about something so much that it comes out of its hiding place.
sentences.main: Curiosity gets the best of it.

parts.meaning: But sometimes

parts.text: curiosity gets the best of it
parts.meaning: it wants to know about something so much that it cannot stop itself

parts.text: and it comes out of hiding.
parts.meaning: and it comes out of its hiding place.

sentences.grammar: "Though" in the middle of a sentence means "but". "Gets the best of it" means the feeling is stronger than the octopus.

sentences.context: Each of its arms, or tentacles, has many suckers, which act like rubber suction cups.
sentences.simple: Each arm of the octopus has many round cups. They work like rubber cups that stick to glass.
sentences.main: Each of its arms has many suckers.

parts.meaning: Every one of its arms
(another name is tentacles)
has many round cups,

parts.text: which act like rubber suction cups.
parts.meaning: and they work like rubber cups that stick to things.

sentences.grammar: Commas around "or tentacles" show an extra name. Jump over it. "Which" here means "and these suckers".

sentences.context: It is nearly impossible to free an object from their grasp.
sentences.simple: It is almost impossible to pull a thing away when the arms hold it.
sentences.main: It is nearly impossible to free an object.

parts.meaning: It is almost impossible
to get a thing out
from the hold of the arms.

sentences.grammar: "It is ... to ..." : the real idea comes after "to". "Their" means "the suckers' (or arms')".

sentences.context: The octopus shot a cloud of black liquid into the water and disappeared into the dark cloud.
sentences.simple: The octopus pushed out a cloud of black liquid into the water and went into the dark cloud, so they could not see it.
sentences.main: The octopus shot a cloud of black liquid and disappeared.

parts.text: The octopus shot a cloud of black liquid into the water
parts.meaning: The octopus pushed out a black cloud into the water

parts.text: and disappeared into the dark cloud.
parts.meaning: and went into the dark cloud, so it was gone.

sentences.grammar: One "who" (the octopus) does two things, joined by "and". "Shot" here does not mean a gun; it means "pushed out very fast".

sentences.context: Sometimes Annie went even faster than Jack, which made him swim faster.
sentences.simple: Sometimes Annie swam faster than Jack, and this made Jack swim faster too.
sentences.main: Annie went even faster than Jack.

parts.text: Sometimes Annie went even faster than Jack,
parts.meaning: Sometimes Annie swam faster than Jack,
and that made Jack swim faster.

sentences.grammar: "Which" here means "and this". It points back to the whole idea before the comma.

sentences.context: But the more Jack floated, the more tired he felt.
sentences.simple: Jack floated for a long time, and he felt more and more tired.

parts.meaning: The longer Jack lay on the water,
the more tired he became.

sentences.grammar: "The more ..., the more ..." means when one thing grows, the other grows too. Look for this pattern.

sentences.context: Then the two dolphins swam smoothly through the water, pulling Jack and Annie toward the reef.
sentences.simple: Then the two dolphins swam easily through the water. They pulled Jack and Annie to the reef.

parts.text: Then the two dolphins swam smoothly through the water,
parts.meaning: Then the two dolphins swam easily through the water,

parts.text: pulling Jack and Annie toward the reef.
parts.job: What they did at the same time.
parts.meaning: and as they swam they pulled Jack and Annie to the reef.

sentences.grammar: The "-ing" part after the comma ("pulling ...") happens at the same time as the main part.

sentences.context: The pearl’s natural beauty makes it a treasure.
sentences.simple: A pearl is beautiful without any help from people, so it is very special and worth a lot.
sentences.main: The beauty makes it a treasure.

parts.meaning: The beauty that the pearl has from nature
makes the pearl very special and worth a lot.

sentences.grammar: "Makes it a treasure" means "turns it into a treasure". The subject is a thing (beauty), not a person.

sentences.context: Sometimes a grain of sand will get between the oyster’s shell and its skin.
sentences.simple: Sometimes a very small piece of sand gets in between the shell and the soft body of the oyster.
sentences.main: A grain of sand will get between the shell and its skin.

parts.meaning: Sometimes a very small piece of sand

parts.text: will get between the oyster’s shell and its skin.
parts.meaning: goes in between the oyster's shell and its body.

sentences.grammar: "Will" here does not mean the future. It means "this often happens".

sentences.context: So it makes a pearly material to surround the grain of sand.
sentences.simple: So the oyster makes a shiny white material all around the small piece of sand.

parts.text: So it makes a pearly material
parts.meaning: So the oyster makes a shiny white material

parts.text: to surround the grain of sand.
parts.meaning: to cover the sand on all sides.

sentences.grammar: "So" at the start means "because of this". "To surround ..." tells you why the oyster makes it.

sentences.context: “You call being squeezed by an octopus and chased by a shark fun?”
sentences.simple: "An octopus held us tightly and a shark ran after us. Do you really call that fun?"

parts.meaning: "Do you call
having an octopus hold us tightly
and having a shark run after us
fun?"

sentences.grammar: This is a question without "do": the question mark and the voice show it. "Being squeezed by" means "an octopus squeezed us".

sentences.context: Then he and Annie slipped up the stairs to change their clothes.
sentences.simple: Then Jack and Annie went up the stairs quickly and quietly to put on dry clothes.
sentences.main: He and Annie slipped up the stairs.

parts.text: Then he and Annie slipped up the stairs
parts.meaning: Then Jack and Annie went up the stairs quickly and quietly
to put on dry clothes.

sentences.grammar: "Slipped" here means "went quickly and quietly", so their mom would not see their wet clothes.

all along.meaning: The whole time, from the beginning.
all along.example: The oyster was on the reef all along.
all along.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

all wet.meaning: 1. Very wet. 2. (American talk) Completely wrong. Jack's notes are wet, and he also feels he did everything wrong.
all wet.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

as well.example: He put that on his list as well.
as well.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

at all.meaning: In any way. "Not ... at all" means "not even a little".
at all.example: There’s nothing plain at all out there.
at all.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

beat it.usageNote: Informal and a little rude. You only need to understand it.

bend down.meaning: To move the top of your body down toward the ground.
bend down.example: Annie bent down to rub her foot.
bend down.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

branch out.meaning: To grow out in different directions from one main line, like the arms of a tree.
branch out.example: Smaller cracks branched out from it.
branch out.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

breast stroke.meaning: A way of swimming. You move your arms and legs out to the sides, like a frog. It makes almost no splash.
breast stroke.example: We better do the breast stroke
breast stroke.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

breathe a sigh of relief.meaning: To let out a long breath because you feel better: a danger or worry is over.
breathe a sigh of relief.example: Jack breathed a sigh of relief.
breathe a sigh of relief.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

build up.meaning: To slowly grow bigger as more and more is added.
build up.example: the reef builds up from stacks of coral skeletons
build up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

catch up with.meaning: To reach someone who is in front of you.
catch up with.example: Had the hammerhead caught up with them?
catch up with.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

check on.meaning: To find out about something, or look at it to make sure it is OK.
check on.example: I’ll have to check on that one
check on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come after.meaning: To follow someone to catch or attack them.
come after.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

come on.meaning: 1. (of a machine) To start working. 2. "Come on!" means "hurry up" or "please do it", or "stop being silly".
come on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

control panel.meaning: A flat board with buttons and switches to work a machine.
control panel.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

dry out.meaning: To become dry after being very wet.
dry out.example: I think I need to rest—and dry out.
dry out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

fade away.meaning: To slowly become weaker until it is gone.
fade away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

figure out.meaning: To think about something until you understand it or find the answer.
figure out.example: It might help us figure out the riddle.
figure out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

fish tank.meaning: A glass box full of water where people keep fish.
fish tank.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

flip through.meaning: To turn the pages of a book quickly, looking for something.
flip through.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

for his life.meaning: "Swim (or run) for your life" means to swim or run as fast as you can to stay alive.
for his life.example: He was swimming for his life
for his life.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

forget it.meaning: Do not think about that now; no.
forget it.example: “Forget it! We have to figure this out!”
forget it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get it right.meaning: To find the right answer; to do something well.
get it right.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get rid of.meaning: To make something go away; to be free of it.
get rid of.example: We’ll never get rid of this thing.
get rid of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

get the best of.meaning: If a feeling gets the best of you, it is too strong and you cannot stop yourself.
get the best of.example: curiosity gets the best of it
get the best of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

get to.meaning: 1. To arrive at a place or at a point. 2. To have the chance to do something.
get to.example: When he got to the page about clams, he read aloud.
get to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

go on.meaning: To happen. "What's going on?" means "What is happening?"
go on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

guess what.meaning: Something you say before you tell surprising news.
guess what.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

hold out.meaning: To move your hand toward someone to give or show them something.
hold out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

in order to.meaning: So that you can; for the purpose of.
in order to.example: in order to gather books through time
in order to.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

in trouble.meaning: In a bad or dangerous situation.
in trouble.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

keep an eye on.example: He just kept his eye on the tree house
keep an eye on.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

leave it alone.meaning: Do not touch it or change it.
leave it alone.example: Maybe we should just leave it alone
leave it alone.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

let go of.example: Jack let go of Annie’s hand.
let go of.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

let out a sigh.meaning: To make a long breathing sound.
let out a sigh.example: Jack let out a huge sigh.
let out a sigh.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

let's go.meaning: "Let's go" means "Let us go": we should go now.
let's go.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

light up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

make it.meaning: 1. To get to a place, or to do something, in spite of problems. 2. "Makes it a treasure" = is the reason that it is a treasure.
make it.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

make up for.meaning: To make a bad thing feel OK by giving something good.
make up for.example: The dolphins made up for everything.
make up for.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

no kidding.meaning: Really! / I agree, that is surprising. (Friendly talk.)
no kidding.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

not one bit.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

out of the corner of his eye.meaning: At the side of what you can see, not right in front of you.
forms: out of the corner of my eye
out of the corner of her eye
out of the corner of your eye
out of the corner of his eye.example: out of the corner of his eye
out of the corner of his eye.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

pick up.meaning: To take something into your hand and lift it.
pick up.example: Annie picked up the riddle scroll.
pick up.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

pull out.meaning: To take something out of a bag, pocket or other place.
pull out.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

put away.meaning: To put something back in its place, or in a bag.
put away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to understand.

right away.usageNote: A common phrase. Good to learn.

sea horse.meaning: A small sea fish with a head shaped like a horse's head.
sea horse.usageNote: You only need to understand it for this story.

ship's log.meaning: A record of a ship's trip, written day by day.
